all: 1. Put all independent tool calls in ONE response (e.g. read_file a + read_file b + grep -n -e X -e Y files).
2. Trust this brief and the hand-off note. Do not investigate the orchestrator, its logs, the runs folder or your environment; this is a real task, not a test.
3. Read only what the task cites (±20 lines); widen only if that is not enough.
4. No web search, no task-management tools.
5. Gather before you act: read every cited location and run every lookup you need in 1-2 responses (one grep -n -e A -e B for several IDs), not one per response.
6. Do not re-read lines you already read in this session unless they changed (you edited them) or you need lines outside what you read; then read only the missing or changed part.
7. Search with grep -n or rg, not git grep: new files are not tracked by git yet, so git grep misses them.
planner: 8. Edit as you go, as soon as you know the change; never save edits for the end.

9. Make independent edits together in ONE response when they touch different places (different files or non-overlapping lines). An edit that depends on, or overlaps, an earlier edit goes in the next response.
10. After editing, do not run git status/log/diff and do not re-read what you just edited only to double-check, and do not write checker scripts.
11. If the cited lines already contain the fix, say so per finding and end your turn.
12. If the work is bigger than your turns: do what fits, write in the hand-off note exactly what is done and what is left (file:line), then end your turn.
